questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with a 3-week history of a painless ulcer on the glans penis with a clean base and indurated, non-tender margins. Inguinal lymph nodes are bilaterally enlarged but non-tender. Which is the most appropriate initial diagnostic test?
questions.exp: The clinical picture—painless, indurated, clean-based genital ulcer with non-tender lymphadenopathy—is classic for primary syphilis (Hunterian chancre). Dark-field microscopy of serum from the ulcer base directly demonstrates Treponema pallidum spirochaetes and is the gold-standard immediate test; VDRL may still be negative at this early stage.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman develops tense bullae on normal-appearing and erythematous skin, predominantly on the flexures and abdomen. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 deposition along the dermoepidermal junction. Which antigen is targeted in this condition?
questions.exp: The clinical and DIF findings describe bullous pemphigoid (BP). BP is caused by autoantibodies against hemidesmosomal proteins BP180 (BPAG2/type XVII collagen) and BP230. The linear IgG+C3 band at the BMZ and tense flexural bullae are hallmarks. Desmoglein 3 and 1 are targets in pemphigus vulgaris/foliaceus; type VII collagen is targeted in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita.

questions.q: A 40-year-old farmer presents with a verrucous, cauliflower-like plaque on the foot following minor trauma 2 years ago. KOH preparation reveals dark-brown, thick-walled, muriform cells (Medlar bodies). What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.exp: The verrucous plaque with muriform (sclerotic) bodies on KOH is pathognomonic of chromoblastomycosis. Fonsecaea pedrosoi is the commonest causative dematiaceous fungus worldwide. Sporothrix causes lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis; Madurella causes mycetoma (grains, not muriform bodies); Alternaria rarely causes opportunistic cutaneous infection.

questions.q: A 22-year-old presents with multiple hypopigmented macules with loss of sensation and a thickened greater auricular nerve. Slit-skin smear is negative. Histopathology shows epithelioid cell granulomas around nerves with no bacilli. What is the Ridley-Jopling classification?
questions.exp: TT leprosy features: few (1–5) well-defined hypopigmented macules, markedly impaired sensation, prominent nerve thickening, negative SSS, and well-formed epithelioid granulomas with lymphocytic infiltration abutting the epidermis on histopathology. This contrasts with BT which may have more lesions and less well-formed granulomas.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman on long-term hydroxychloroquine for discoid lupus develops blurring of vision. Ophthalmological examination reveals a 'bull's-eye' maculopathy. What is the mechanism of retinal toxicity?
opts: Accumulation in melanin-containing retinal pigment epithelium causing photoreceptor damage
Inhibition of VEGF leading to retinal ischaemia
Direct mitochondrial toxicity to ganglion cells
questions.exp: Hydroxychloroquine binds avidly to melanin in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), accumulates over time, and causes lysosomal dysfunction leading to photoreceptor apoptosis. The characteristic parafoveal 'bull's-eye' pattern on fundoscopy and OCT corresponds to RPE and photoreceptor loss in this zone. Baseline and annual ophthalmological screening is mandatory.

questions.q: A 32-year-old man presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base in a dermatomal distribution on the trunk, following a prodrome of burning pain. Two days later, he develops new lesions. Which antiviral and dosing regimen is most appropriate?
opts: Acyclovir 800 mg five times daily for 7 days
Acyclovir 200 mg five times daily for 5 days
Valacyclovir 500 mg twice daily for 5 days
Famciclovir 125 mg twice daily for 5 days
questions.exp: Herpes zoster treatment requires high-dose acyclovir: 800 mg five times daily (every 4 h omitting the night dose) for 7 days. Acyclovir 200 mg five times daily is the dose for primary genital herpes. Valacyclovir 1000 mg TDS for 7 days or famciclovir 500 mg TDS for 7 days are alternatives—the low doses listed in options C and D are incorrect for zoster.

questions.q: A 65-year-old man with a history of arsenic exposure presents with multiple, bilateral, non-tender keratotic plaques on the palms and soles, and Mees' lines on nails. Skin biopsy of a warty plaque on the trunk shows full-thickness epidermal dysplasia. What is the diagnosis of the trunk lesion?
questions.exp: Chronic arsenicism causes arsenical keratoses (palmoplantar), Mees' lines (transverse white nail bands), rain-drop pigmentation, and multiple Bowen's disease lesions (squamous cell carcinoma in situ) on non-sun-exposed sites. Full-thickness epidermal dysplasia is the hallmark of Bowen's disease. AK affects sun-exposed skin and shows partial-thickness dysplasia.

questions.q: A 19-year-old woman presents with a targetoid lesion on the palm, ulcers on the buccal mucosa, and crusted lips after starting a course of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. She has no skin detachment. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: Discontinue the causative drug and start supportive care with systemic corticosteroids
Continue the drug and add antihistamines
Discontinue the drug, start intravenous immunoglobulin
Perform skin biopsy before any treatment
questions.exp: Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) is characterised by targetoid lesions, mucosal involvement, and <10% body surface area detachment. The first step is immediate discontinuation of the offending drug (sulfonamides are a common trigger). Supportive care in a burns unit/ICU and systemic corticosteroids (early short course) or IVIG are used; corticosteroids are appropriate here given early presentation. IVIG is preferred in TEN or rapidly progressive SJS.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man presents with well-demarcated, silvery-scaled plaques on the extensor surfaces of elbows and knees, scalp, and nails showing pitting and onycholysis. Which cytokine is primarily responsible for keratinocyte hyperproliferation in psoriasis?
questions.exp: The IL-23/Th17 axis is central to psoriasis pathogenesis. IL-23 (from dendritic cells/macrophages) drives Th17 differentiation, which produces IL-17A. IL-17A acts on keratinocytes to induce hyperproliferation, antimicrobial peptide production (β-defensins, S100 proteins), and chemokine secretion recruiting neutrophils. Biologics targeting IL-17A (secukinumab, ixekizumab) and IL-17RA (brodalumab) are effective treatments.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with Raynaud's phenomenon, puffy fingers, and progressive skin tightening of the fingers and forearms for 6 months. ANA is positive (1:320, speckled). Which specific antibody is most likely to be positive and portends a risk of pulmonary arterial hypertension?
questions.exp: The speckled ANA pattern with Raynaud's and limited skin involvement (fingers/forearms) suggests limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc), previously CREST syndrome. ACA is positive in ~70–80% of lcSSc and is strongly associated with pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) and calcinosis. Anti-Scl-70 is associated with diffuse SSc and pulmonary fibrosis; anti-RNA pol III with diffuse SSc and renal crisis; anti-Jo-1 with polymyositis.

questions.q: A 5-year-old child has a 4-cm annular, boggy, fluctuant scalp swelling with overlying alopecia and scattered pustules. Regional cervical lymph nodes are enlarged. Which treatment is most appropriate?
opts: Oral griseofulvin for 6–8 weeks plus topical antifungal shampoo
questions.exp: The boggy, pustular scalp swelling with alopecia in a child is a kerion—an intense inflammatory reaction to tinea capitis (usually Trichophyton violaceum/T. tonsurans in India). Systemic antifungal is mandatory; griseofulvin (10–20 mg/kg/day) for 6–8 weeks is the standard therapy. Topical antifungals do not penetrate the hair shaft. I&D is harmful (may worsen scarring). Adjunct selenium sulfide or ketoconazole shampoo reduces spore shedding.

questions.q: A 25-year-old man presents with multiple painless ulcers on the penis and perianal region. Biopsy reveals pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia with large histiocytes containing intracytoplasmic Donovan bodies. What is the treatment of choice?
opts: Azithromycin 1 g weekly for at least 3 weeks
Benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM single dose
Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 21 days
Ciprofloxacin 750 mg twice daily for 3 weeks
questions.exp: Donovanosis (granuloma inguinale) caused by Klebsiella granulomatis shows Donovan bodies within macrophages. The CDC-recommended first-line regimen is azithromycin 1 g orally once weekly (or 500 mg daily) for at least 3 weeks and until lesions have healed completely. Doxycycline is an alternative but not the current first-line. Benzathine penicillin is for syphilis.

questions.q: A 68-year-old man presents with a pearly, translucent papule with telangiectasias and a rolled edge on the inner canthus of the left eye. On dermoscopy, arborising vessels are seen. What is the most likely diagnosis and the preferred treatment?
opts: Nodular basal cell carcinoma; Mohs micrographic surgery
Squamous cell carcinoma; wide local excision
questions.exp: The pearly papule with rolled edges, telangiectasias, and arborising vessels on dermoscopy is classic for nodular BCC. Periocular BCC (especially medial canthus) carries a high recurrence risk due to complex anatomy. Mohs micrographic surgery provides the highest cure rate (>99%) with maximal tissue conservation, making it the preferred treatment for this site.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman with SLE develops an urticarial rash that persists >24 hours, leaving post-inflammatory pigmentation, and bilateral ankle oedema. Biopsy shows perivascular neutrophilic infiltrate with leukocytoclasis and fibrinoid necrosis of vessel walls. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Urticarial vasculitis presents as urticarial lesions lasting >24 hours (vs. ordinary urticaria <24 h), often with bruising/pigmentation. Biopsy confirms small-vessel vasculitis (leukocytoclasia + fibrinoid necrosis). It is associated with SLE (hypocomplementaemic urticarial vasculitis syndrome), hepatitis B/C. Differentiated from chronic urticaria by lesion duration and histopathology.

questions.q: A 20-year-old woman with a history of atopy develops erythema and blistering on photo-exposed areas after taking a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug. The reaction heals with hyperpigmentation confined to sun-exposed sites. Which type of photosensitivity reaction is this?
questions.exp: A phototoxic reaction is a non-immunological, dose-dependent reaction occurring on first exposure in virtually anyone. It manifests as exaggerated sunburn (erythema, blistering) confined strictly to UV-exposed sites and heals with hyperpigmentation. Photoallergy is immunologically mediated (requires prior sensitisation), can spread beyond exposed areas, and presents as eczematous lesions. NSAIDs (particularly piroxicam, ketoprofen) are classic phototoxins.

questions.q: A neonate presents at birth with generalised blistering. Electron microscopy reveals cleavage within the lamina lucida of the basement membrane zone. Immunofluorescence mapping shows absence of staining for laminin-332. What is the subtype of epidermolysis bullosa?
questions.exp: Junctional EB (JEB) Herlitz type (lethal) shows cleavage in the lamina lucida, caused by mutations in LAMA3, LAMB3, or LAMC2 (genes encoding laminin-332). Immunofluorescence mapping confirms absent laminin-332. EB simplex cleaves within the epidermis (above the BMZ); dystrophic EB cleaves below the lamina densa (anchoring fibrils, type VII collagen). Herlitz JEB is severe and often lethal in infancy.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man from Bihar presents with fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, and skin darkening (post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis suspected on clinical grounds). Which investigation confirms PKDL?
opts: Slit-skin smear or skin biopsy showing amastigotes
Bone marrow aspiration for Leishman-Donovan bodies
Polymerase chain reaction of peripheral blood
questions.exp: PKDL is diagnosed by demonstrating Leishmania amastigotes in slit-skin smear or skin biopsy of the hypopigmented/erythematous patches. Bone marrow aspiration is for active VL; rK39 may be positive but is not specific for PKDL; PCR of skin biopsy is a sensitive alternative but slit-skin smear is the standard accessible test in India.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman presents with a pigmented lesion on the sole. Dermoscopy shows a parallel ridge pattern. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Acral lentiginous melanoma (ALM) characteristically shows the parallel ridge pattern on dermoscopy—pigment runs along the ridges of the dermatoglyphics (where eccrine ducts open). Benign acral naevi show the parallel furrow pattern (pigment in the sulci). Plantar wart shows interrupted dermatoglyphics. The parallel ridge pattern has a sensitivity of ~86% and specificity of ~99% for ALM.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about dapsone is correct regarding its mechanism of action in leprosy?
opts: It inhibits dihydropteroate synthase, blocking folate synthesis in Mycobacterium leprae
It binds to the 50S ribosomal subunit inhibiting protein synthesis
It chelates iron, preventing bacterial growth
questions.exp: Dapsone (a sulphone) is a bacteriostatic agent that competitively inhibits dihydropteroate synthase (DHPS), the enzyme that incorporates PABA into dihydropteroic acid. This blocks folate synthesis in susceptible bacteria including M. leprae. Its mechanism is analogous to sulphonamides. Resistance arises from mutations in the folP1 gene encoding DHPS.

questions.q: A 38-year-old man presents with a 2-year history of pruritic, intensely itchy papules and vesicles on the extensor surfaces of elbows, knees, buttocks, and scalp. He also reports intermittent diarrhoea and bloating. IgA endomysial antibodies are positive. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.exp: The intensely pruritic vesicles on extensor sites with positive IgA endomysial antibodies (against epidermal transglutaminase) confirm dermatitis herpetiformis (DH), associated with coeliac disease. Dapsone 50–100 mg/day provides rapid symptom relief (within 24–48 h). A strict, lifelong gluten-free diet is equally important—it controls both the gut disease and, over months, reduces dapsone requirements.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with a rapidly enlarging, firm, erythematous nodule on the forearm with central ulceration, developing over 6 weeks. Histopathology shows pleomorphic squamous cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, atypical mitoses, and keratin pearl formation invading the dermis. Which histological feature indicates poor prognosis?
opts: Tumour thickness > 2 mm and perineural invasion
questions.exp: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) poor-prognosis features include: tumour thickness >2 mm, Clark level ≥IV, perineural invasion, lymphovascular invasion, poor differentiation, location (ear, lip), size >2 cm, and immunosuppression. Perineural invasion specifically is associated with recurrence and nodal metastasis. Keratin pearls indicate differentiation (relatively better prognosis) not worse.

questions.q: A 72-year-old woman presents with blistering predominantly in the oral cavity, followed by flaccid bullae on the skin that rupture easily, leaving raw erosions. Nikolsky sign is positive. DIF shows intercellular IgG deposition ('chicken-wire' pattern). Serology is positive for anti-desmoglein 3. What is the first-line systemic treatment?
opts: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day as initial monotherapy or with azathioprine
Rituximab 375 mg/m² weekly for 4 weeks as first-line
questions.exp: This is pemphigus vulgaris (mucosal-dominant type) indicated by predominant oral erosions, positive Nikolsky sign, intercellular IgG DIF, and anti-Dsg3. The cornerstone of treatment remains systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day). A steroid-sparing agent (azathioprine or mycophenolate mofetil) is added early. Rituximab has emerged as an excellent option and in some guidelines is now a first-line alternative for moderate-severe PV, but standard first-line remains prednisolone ± azathioprine in most Indian settings.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman with vitiligo affecting 10% BSA (face and hands) wants the most effective treatment to repigment her lesions. Which modality has the highest repigmentation rate for generalised vitiligo?
questions.exp: NB-UVB (311 nm) is the current gold-standard phototherapy for active and stable generalised vitiligo, achieving >75% repigmentation in ~50–70% of patients, particularly on the face and trunk. It stimulates melanocyte migration from follicular reservoirs and modulates the immune response. Topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus) are effective on the face/neck (acral and segmental are less responsive). Hydroquinone is a depigmenting agent used for hyperpigmentation, not vitiligo treatment.

questions.q: A 16-year-old presents with comedones, papules, and pustules on the face. He is started on topical tretinoin. After 3 weeks he returns with increased redness and peeling of the skin. What is this phenomenon called and what is the appropriate action?
opts: Retinoid dermatitis (purging reaction); reassure and continue at a lower frequency
Rosacea exacerbation; switch to azelaic acid
questions.exp: Retinoid dermatitis (sometimes called 'retinoid flare' or 'purging') is an expected irritant reaction to topical retinoids occurring in the first 4–6 weeks. It manifests as erythema, scaling, and increased acne lesions. Patients should be counselled beforehand and managed by reducing frequency of application (alternate nights), using moisturiser, and gentle cleansers. Stopping the drug is usually unnecessary; the reaction subsides with continued use.

questions.q: A 48-year-old HIV-positive man (CD4 count 80 cells/μL) presents with multiple hyperpigmented papules and nodules on the skin, trunk, and oral mucosa. Biopsy shows proliferating spindle cells with slit-like vascular spaces and extravasated red cells. What is the causative virus?
questions.exp: AIDS-associated Kaposi sarcoma is caused by HHV-8 (Kaposi sarcoma herpesvirus). The spindle-cell proliferation with vascular slits and haemosiderin is classic histopathology. HHV-8 is necessary but not sufficient—immunosuppression (HIV) allows unrestricted viral replication. Treatment includes ART, liposomal doxorubicin, paclitaxel, and intralesional vinblastine for localised lesions.

questions.q: During a Wood's lamp examination, a patient's hypopigmented patches on the face fluoresce bright blue-white. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Vitiligo lesions show a striking bright blue-white (chalk-white) fluorescence under Wood's lamp (365 nm) due to complete absence of melanin, which normally absorbs UV. This makes lesions far more visible, especially in fair-skinned patients. Pityriasis versicolor shows yellow-green fluorescence. Ash-leaf macules of tuberous sclerosis accentuate (glow) under Wood's lamp but are not bright blue-white. Leprosy lesions do not fluoresce distinctly.

questions.q: A dermatologist performs a shave biopsy of a 4-mm tan nodule on the back. Histopathology reports melanoma with Breslow thickness of 1.2 mm, no ulceration, and mitotic rate <1/mm². According to the AJCC 8th edition staging, what is the recommended surgical margin for wide local excision?
questions.exp: AJCC 8th edition guidelines for melanoma WLE margins: Breslow ≤1.0 mm → 1 cm; 1.01–2.0 mm → 1–2 cm (most guidelines 1 cm is acceptable, but 1–2 cm is recommended); >2 mm → 2 cm. For T2a (1.01–2.0 mm, no ulceration) a 1–2 cm margin is standard; the minimum acceptable and commonly used margin in this thickness range is 1 cm. Sentinel lymph node biopsy should be discussed for Breslow >0.8 mm.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man presents with erythematous, scaling, annular plaques on the trunk and extremities for 6 months. Woods lamp shows no fluorescence. KOH of scale is negative. Biopsy shows lichenoid infiltrate at the dermoepidermal junction with interface change and civatte bodies. Which condition fits best?
questions.exp: Lichen planus (LP) classically shows lichenoid (band-like) lymphocytic infiltrate at the DEJ, interface vacuolar change, saw-tooth rete ridges, and civatte (colloid/hyaline) bodies (apoptotic keratinocytes). Annular LP on the trunk is a recognised variant. Tinea would show hyphae on KOH; SCLE would show positive ANA/anti-Ro; nummular eczema shows spongiosis not interface change.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman is diagnosed with localised morphoea on the trunk. Which investigation helps differentiate morphoea from systemic sclerosis (SSc)?
opts: Anti-centromere and anti-Scl-70 antibodies are absent in morphoea but may be positive in SSc
Capillaroscopy shows dilated capillaries in morphoea
Morphoea involves face and acral skin more than trunk
Raynaud's phenomenon is characteristic of morphoea
questions.exp: Morphoea is localised fibrosing disorder of skin without systemic features. Anti-Scl-70, ACA, anti-RNA pol III are negative in morphoea but may be positive in systemic sclerosis. Capillaroscopic abnormalities (dilated loops, avascular areas) are hallmarks of SSc, not morphoea. Raynaud's and acral/facial involvement are features of SSc, not morphoea.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with a 1-cm tender nodule at the lateral aspect of her right eyebrow that has been growing for 3 months. It has a smooth surface, normal overlying skin, and a soft-to-firm consistency. FNA yields cheesy material. Histopathology shows a cyst lined by stratified squamous epithelium with a granular cell layer and filled with laminated keratin. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: An epidermal inclusion cyst (EIC) is lined by true stratified squamous epithelium with a granular layer, and is filled with laminated keratin ('cheesy' material). It originates from the follicular infundibulum. Trichilemmal cysts lack a granular layer (trichilemmal keratinisation), contain homogeneous keratin, and are usually on the scalp. Dermoid cysts contain skin appendages. Steatocystoma is lined by a thin layer with sebaceous gland lobules.

questions.q: A 22-year-old man undergoes patch testing. After 48 hours, patch test to nickel sulfate shows a ++reaction (erythema, papules, and vesicles confined to the test site). What type of hypersensitivity reaction underlies this?
questions.exp: Allergic contact dermatitis (ACD), tested by patch testing, is a classic Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity reaction mediated by sensitised Th1 CD4+ lymphocytes (and CD8+ cytotoxic T cells in some haptens). The reaction occurs 48–96 hours after exposure. Nickel is the commonest contact allergen worldwide. Type I reactions (urticaria, anaphylaxis) are IgE-mediated and occur within minutes.
